To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the performance of a speaker verification algorithm is strongly affected by the amount of training data used to train the recognition engine, (b) the performance of the algorithm is strongly affected, in the case of conversational telephone data, by the amount of mismatch between the training and the test data (in particular, handset or channel mismatch), (c) the performance of an algorithm that uses a recognition engine to score the utterance is strongly affected by whether or not the recognition engine is given access

a system based on a continuous speech recognition engine is a promising approach to telephone speaker verification, and that performance depends on the quality of the speech recognition engine and on the amount of mismatch between training and test data.

speaker verification performance is significantly degraded when there is a channel mismatch between training and test data, that the degradation is less for long test utterances, that the performance is not improved by transcribing the training data, and that the performance is improved when the recognition system is trained on data with the same channel characteristics as the test data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a speaker verification engine based on a large vocabulary speech recognition system.
the problem of speaker verification using continuous speech.
the use of speech recognition techniques to provide the basis for a speaker verification system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

speaker verification performance is strongly influenced by the quality of the speech recognition system used to obtain the word sequences, and that a good speech recognizer is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for a good speaker verifier.

a speaker verification system using a large vocabulary speech recognition front end can be made to work, but it is not yet as robust as the best speaker verification systems using a smaller vocabulary.
the performance of speaker verification systems is limited by the mismatch between the training and test conditions, and that this can be reduced by careful design of the training set.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

speaker verification through large vocabulary speech recognition is a viable alternative to the more traditional approaches, and that it has some advantages in terms of robustness to channel and handset mismatch.

we are able to achieve performance on telephone speech that is comparable to that on read text, and that we have shown that a large vocabulary continuous speech recogniser can be used as a speaker verification front end with little loss of performance.

the use of a large vocabulary recognition engine to provide the acoustic features for a speaker verification system has a significant advantage over the conventional approach of using a small vocabulary recognition engine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a speaker verification system based on large vocabulary continuous speech can perform as well as, or better than, systems based on isolated word recognition.
a large-vocabulary recognition system is a viable alternative to a small-vocabulary system for speaker verification.

a speaker verification system built around a large-vocabulary continuous-speech recognition engine is a viable option, and that such a system can achieve good performance on a conversational telephone speech test set.
